items.title: Cosa è successo a Milano in due giorni di saccheggi e disordini
items.summary: Gruppi di ragazzi, molti dei quali minorenni, hanno distrutto alcune vetrine in centro e si sono scontrati con la polizia
items.content:
Sabato e domenica pomeriggio centinaia di persone, in gran parte a volto coperto, hanno distrutto oggetti, devastato alcuni negozi con atti vandalici e saccheggi nelle principali vie del centro di Milano. Le forze dell’ordine hanno tentato di bloccare i disordini con la forza, usando anche lacrimogeni e idranti, ma ci sono riuscite solo dopo diverse ore, dimostrando una certa impreparazione di fronte a gruppi che hanno agito perlopiù in modo spontaneo, confuso e disorganizzato. In due giorni sono state fermate e arrestate decine di persone, in gran parte minorenni , e comunque tutte molto giovani.

Nelle vie tra piazza Duomo, via Torino e il Castello Sforzesco sono stati saccheggiati alcuni punti vendita di catene di abbigliamento, sfondate una decina di vetrine e quattro pensiline del tram. Tra Brera e Buenos Aires sono avvenuti un paio di altri saccheggi e alcuni atti vandalici più isolati.

Le devastazioni di sabato sono iniziate mentre era in corso la manifestazione “Italia in piazza” contro il caro vita, cioè l’aumento dei prezzi di prodotti e servizi avvenuto negli ultimi anni. I manifestanti, in gran parte studenti, si erano organizzati online, soprattutto su TikTok, dandosi appuntamento per le 15 in piazza Duomo.

I primi scontri c’erano stati poco dopo l’inizio del corteo, quando le persone erano state bloccate dalla polizia in via Broletto, una strada molto stretta tra il Duomo e il Castello Sforzesco. Qui e nella via laterale di San Prospero, dopo alcuni lanci di sassi e bottiglie, la polizia aveva caricato la testa della manifestazione manganellando e buttando a terra alcuni ragazzi.

Le persone sono rimaste bloccate in via Broletto per circa un’ora. A quel punto il corteo si era diviso, in parte dietro e in parte davanti alla polizia, e i manifestanti che non riuscivano ad avanzare hanno deviato per altre vie, raggiungendo prima largo Cairoli, davanti al Castello Sforzesco, e poi il cimitero Monumentale.

Mentre il corteo manifestava pacificamente, gruppi di persone incappucciate hanno iniziato a vandalizzare strade e alcuni negozi del centro, tra Duomo, corso Vittorio Emanuele, piazza dei Mercanti e San Babila. Il negozio di scarpe Foot Locker in corso Vittorio Emanuele II è stato saccheggiato. Sono state distrutte anche le vetrate di alcune fermate del tram. Le persone hanno spaccato alcune vetrine, distrutto dehors, appiccato incendi e rovesciato cestini mentre lanciavano bottiglie, sassi, bombe carta, petardi, sedie e altri oggetti contro le auto delle forze dell’ordine e contro gli agenti.

Il dirigente di polizia Angelo De Simone, che era in strada a indirizzare le operazioni degli agenti, è stato colpito in testa da una pietra, che gli ha provocato una piccola ferita. La polizia ha inseguito e caricato le persone, colpendone diverse con manganellate, e ha cercato di disperderle con un idrante. Nel complesso le forze dell’ordine hanno faticato a gestire i violenti, che agivano senza un coordinamento. Non appartenevano a organizzazioni, collettivi studenteschi o centri sociali.

Molti residenti e turisti sono rimasti bloccati all’interno dei locali in cui si erano rifugiati e della stazione della metropolitana di Duomo, che è stata chiusa. Durante gli scontri Mario Delpini, l’arcivescovo di Milano, stava tenendo una celebrazione all’interno del Duomo, alla fine della quale i fedeli sono stati evacuati attraverso un passaggio sotterraneo che conduce a un’uscita su piazza Fontana.

Alla fine della giornata di sabato la polizia ha fermato 72 persone, denunciandone 22 e arrestandone 12, cinque delle quali minorenni.

Le devastazioni sono ricominciate domenica pomeriggio , quando poco prima delle 17, tra piazza Duomo e via Torino, gruppi di ragazzi con il volto coperto hanno ripreso a lanciare cestini e oggetti contro le vetrine dei negozi e in mezzo alla strada. I ragazzi erano perlopiù minorenni, sia di origine italiana sia di seconda generazione, provenienti dalle periferie e dall’hinterland.

Hanno preso d’assalto e saccheggiato il supermercato Carrefour di via Torino, rubando cibo e alcolici. Dopo l’intervento delle forze dell’ordine la situazione sembrava essere tornata sotto controllo, ma gli scontri sono poi ripresi tra piazza Duomo e piazza dei Mercanti, con lanci di sassi e bombe carta a cui la polizia rispondeva con lacrimogeni.

La fermata della metropolitana del Duomo è stata nuovamente chiusa e le visite turistiche alla cattedrale sono state interrotte anticipatamente. Gli scontri sono proseguiti in via Torino, dove sono state spaccate pensiline dei tram, buttati a terra motorini, ribaltati tavolini e cestini.

In via Orefici sono state distrutte le vetrine di Levi’s, di Under Armour e della profumeria Perlier, in via Dante quelle di Store Enel e in Corso Buenos Aires della sartoria Luigi Fusaro, dove due responsabili dicono che i ragazzi si sono portati via il registratore di cassa con l’incasso della giornata.

Ragazzi incappucciati hanno poi spaccato le vetrine di Decathlon in piazza Castello (dove è stato anche appiccato un piccolo fuoco, vicino alla fontana) e hanno saccheggiato il negozio. In alcuni video li si vede portare via vestiti, scarpe e biciclette. Un negozio Vodafone è stato assaltato ed è stato portato via un estintore. Ci sono stati disordini anche tra via Moscova, largo La Foppa e corso Garibaldi.

In serata è stata spaccata una vetrina della Rinascente in piazza Duomo, sono stati lanciati sassi contro le vetrine di McDonald’s, e rovesciati cestini nella piazza davanti al Teatro alla Scala. La polizia, inizialmente schierata in Duomo, ha cercato di inseguire i ragazzi, che però si sono mossi velocemente tra le vie del centro, disperdendosi tra le zone di Cordusio, Cinque Vie e il Castello Sforzesco.

Anche domenica la polizia ha avuto difficoltà a gestire la situazione, nonostante quanto successo il giorno prima: è riuscita a fermare solo piccoli gruppi di persone tra via Torino e San Babila, picchiando qualcuno con i manganelli, e ha disperso i violenti dopo diverse ore. Sabato il sindaco di Milano Beppe Sala aveva già suggerito che la presenza delle forze dell’ordine fosse troppo scarsa, scontrandosi con il ministro dell’Interno Matteo Piantedosi. Alla fine domenica sono stati fermati più di 200 ragazzi e 160 sono stati portati in questura: secondo la polizia circa l’80 per cento è minorenne.

items.title: Un aereo partito da Israele e diretto in Austria ha fatto un atterraggio d’emergenza in Bulgaria per un allarme bomba
items.content:
Domenica sera un aereo della compagnia Austrian Airlines, partito da Tel Aviv in Israele e diretto a Vienna in Austria, è stato costretto a un atterraggio d’emergenza a Sofia, capitale della Bulgaria, dopo che l’equipaggio aveva ricevuto un allarme bomba. A bordo dell’Airbus A320 c’erano 51 passeggeri e 6 membri dell’equipaggio.

Secondo il ministero dei Trasporti bulgaro, l’allarme è arrivato mentre l’aereo si trovava vicino al confine con la Romania. Un caccia MiG-29 dell’aeronautica militare bulgara è decollato per scortare l’aereo fino all’aeroporto di Sofia, dove è atterrato senza problemi. Tutte le persone a bordo sono state fatte scendere e l’aereo è stato sottoposto a controlli di sicurezza. Le autorità bulgare hanno aperto un’indagine per accertare l’origine dell’allarme.

items.title: Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut aid to Gaza
items.summary: The number of people helped by the UN agency in the Palestinian territory will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
items.content:
One of the main suppliers of food aid to the Gaza Strip, the World Food Programme (WFP), says that it is being forced to "drastically reduce lifesaving assistance" to the Palestinian territory due to funding shortages.

Overall, the number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.

The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves.

One effect is that the number of hot meals that are currently being provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day.

Families living in hard-to-reach areas, for example near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates Israel's area of military control, will receive a meal every other day instead of daily.

Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced and two-thirds rely on food aid to survive.

"It's a disaster! What will we do with these reduced rations? How will we provide for the little ones?" said Mervat al-Satari, a displaced Palestinian mother-of-five at a camp in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis after being told of the WFP's news. "Sometimes we wait for these meals to eat."

"This will affect us a lot. The daily aid was somehow ticking the box but now it will be every two days," said Sawsan Bahloul, who is also from al-Mawasi and is a mother of three. She added that the portions given by the community kitchen - usually pasta or lentils with occasional potatoes and aubergines - were already too small to feed her family.

The Palestine director for the WFP, Shaun Hughes, is clear that the cuts are being made because of finances, and "not because the needs are coming down, or because we don't have access - we do."

Already, since July, there have been reductions in cash transfers provided to some half a million people, meaning they have less money to buy food in local markets. The number of Gazans given bags of flour and ration boxes by the WFP will now fall from 1.1 million to 600,000 each month.

The WFP received less than half as much funding for its Palestinian operations in 2026 as in previous years. The agency says it urgently needs $450m (£338m) to maintain "critical" operations over the next six months.

Despite a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel that was agreed a year ago, violence has continued, including almost daily Israeli strikes, and humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire.

There has been no reconstruction and little recovery, with Israel tightly controlling the entry of goods through crossings. While food markets are now well stocked, few can afford to buy from them. More than 80% of people in Gaza are unemployed so most of the population relies on aid.

Families currently receiving the WFP food handouts complained to the BBC that already these were insufficient and gave them little diversity in their diets.

"The flour isn't enough and the food boxes aren't enough either," said Dalal al-Dahdouh, who is living in the ruins of her home in Gaza City with her family of eight. She fears the new cuts will have "a major impact".

The mother draws a contrast between the current desperate situation and life before the war. "In the past, thank God, we had our own home and a wonderful life. We had fresh vegetables, proper sanitation facilities and our own land," she said. "Now we live entirely on aid, including WFP vouchers."

There is no cooking gas available in Gaza because the Israeli government considers it a "dual use" item that could be used by Hamas for military purposes. Wood is expensive, so many families send their children into the street to find plastic and cardboard to burn as fuel to make bread or heat food.

"It's still a very concerning humanitarian situation, people living in brutal conditions, most people still without a proper home, living in tents, poor access to water and sanitation and healthcare," Hughes of the WFP told the BBC. "Cuts to food assistance are going to compound that hardship that families have been facing for three years now."

Humanitarian workers say that despite a modest improvement in Gaza compared to a year ago, acute food insecurity and the risk of famine returning continue to loom over the territory.

In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) - the world's foremost experts on food security - reported that two-thirds of the population - 1.4 million people - were "expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026".

For now, the WFP says it can continue supporting bakeries that provide one-third of Gaza's bread needs and provide nutritional assistance to about 300,000 women and children. It also delivers health food snacks to some 200,000 children.

In the occupied West Bank, the WFP is continuing to give assistance to some 200,000 Palestinians, having halved the number of recipients in September.

The agency says food insecurity is rising in the territory mostly due to increased Israeli settler violence and Palestinian displacement.

items.title: Tmux and Claude Code: Sessions, Send-Keys, and the Ceiling
items.summary: Article URL: https://crystl.dev/guides/tmux-for-ai-agents/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50148855 Points: 39 # Comments: 21
items.content:
tmux runs your AI coding agents in named, detachable sessions that survive a closed terminal or a dropped SSH connection. You get one window holding many agents, send-keys to type into any of them from a script, and capture-pane to read one back. That combination is why people use it.

Before you build any of it by hand, check the built-in path: recent versions of Claude Code can create the worktree and the tmux session for you with claude --worktree --tmux . This guide covers that first, then everything it doesn’t reach, then the point where tmux itself stops.

A coding agent is a long-running process that wants to keep talking to a terminal. Three properties of tmux match that shape:

It survives disconnection. The tmux server owns the pty, not your terminal window. Close the window, lose your SSH link, put the laptop to sleep: the agent keeps working and is still there when you reattach.

It holds many sessions in one window. Four agents become four named sessions you switch between with a keystroke, instead of four windows you hunt for in the app switcher.

It’s scriptable from outside. Any shell, anywhere, can type into a running agent or read its screen. No IPC to build, no API to wire up. This is the property people build on, and it’s why tmux keeps showing up in agent-orchestration scripts.

Claude Code ships with this wired up for the single-agent-on-a-branch case. Two flags, from claude --help on a recent version:

So the whole “isolate this task, give it its own session” move is one command:

Two details matter before you rely on it. --tmux errors without --worktree , so it’s a worktree feature that happens to make a session, not a general session flag. And on iTerm2 it uses native panes instead of tmux, which is nicer to look at and means the tmux commands in the rest of this page have nothing to attach to. Pass --tmux=classic when you want real tmux underneath, which you do if you plan to script against the session.

For a single agent on a single branch, that’s the answer. Use it and skip ahead.

What it doesn’t do: run several agents in one session, lay out panes so you can watch them, let you type into a running agent from a script, tell you which agent is waiting on you, or set any of this up on a remote box over SSH. Those are the rest of this guide, and each one is where people end up writing tmux by hand.

More on the worktree half of that flag in git worktrees for parallel development .

The organizing rule that keeps this usable: one tmux session per repo, named after the repo. Not per task, not per agent. Tasks come and go; the project is the stable thing.

-A is attach-or-create. It makes a single command safe to run repeatedly, which is what you want in a shell function:

Session names can’t contain . or : (tmux uses them as target separators), hence the tr .

Inside a session, give each agent its own window, named for the task:

Windows are better than panes for agents you’re not actively watching, because a window costs no screen space. Panes are for the two or three you want side by side right now:

#{pane_current_path} is easy to leave off. Without it a new pane opens in the directory the session started in, not the directory you’re actually in, and the agent you launch there is pointed at the wrong repo.

Two layouts by name: tiled for an even grid of agents, and main-vertical for one big pane (the agent you’re driving) with the rest stacked beside it.

Percentage values for main-pane-width need tmux 3.2 or newer. On older builds use an absolute column count ( main-pane-width 120 ). Check with tmux -V .

These are the lines that matter for agent work specifically. They’re not a full config, they’re the delta from defaults that a fleet of agents makes you want.

Agent TUIs like to set the terminal title, so without allow-rename off your carefully named auth window becomes whatever the agent felt like calling itself.

escape-time 10 fixes the “my arrow keys are laggy inside the agent” complaint. The default delay exists to disambiguate a real Escape key from an escape sequence, and it makes interactive TUIs feel mushy.

send-keys types into a pane as if you were at the keyboard. This is how you script an agent from cron, from a git hook, or from another agent.

Bare arguments get interpreted as key names. Enter , C-c , Escape , and Space are keys, not text. If your prompt contains one of those words as a standalone argument it gets sent as a keypress. Use -l to send a literal string:

-l disables key-name lookup entirely, so the newline has to be a second call.

Semicolons end the tmux command. A trailing ; in your text is read as a command separator. Escape it as \; .

Agent TUIs need a beat between the text and the newline. Many agent input boxes debounce or re-render on paste, and an Enter arriving in the same frame as the text gets swallowed. The reliable pattern:

capture-pane dumps a pane’s contents to stdout. It’s the read half of the pair.

-J matters more than it looks. Without it, a line that wrapped at your terminal width comes back as two lines, and every grep you write against the output is wrong at the seams.

For a continuous log rather than a snapshot, pipe-pane streams everything a pane produces to a command:

-o toggles, so running it twice turns it off. The output is raw, escape sequences and all, so pipe it through something like sed -E 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*[a-zA-Z]//g' if you want it readable later.

Every person who runs several agents in tmux eventually builds this: a status line that tells you which agents are working and which are waiting.

The mechanism is #() in the status line, which runs a shell command and interpolates its output, refreshed every status-interval seconds.

And the script, which capture-scrapes each pane for a sign of life:

It works, and it’s worth building. Be clear-eyed about what it’s doing: string matching against a TUI’s rendered frame, on a five-second poll, for every pane you have open. The match strings are whatever your agent version happens to print this week.

The lighter-weight version uses tmux’s own activity tracking instead of scraping. monitor-silence fires an alert when a pane produces no output for N seconds, which is the closest native signal to “this agent stopped”:

Silence is a proxy for done, not a report of it. An agent thinking hard about a large file is silent too.

The tmux server is just a process owned by your user. Nothing about tmux makes it survive a reboot, and a session’s scrollback is lost when the server stops. If the transcript matters, pipe-pane it to a file or use a tool that persists history on its own.

One detail people trip on: a detached session’s panes are sized to the last client that was attached, or to 80x24 if there never was one. An agent TUI rendering into an 80-column pane while you’re away will look wrong when you reattach at 200 columns, until it redraws. set-window-option -g aggressive-resize on helps when several clients are attached at different sizes.

This is where tmux is genuinely hard to replace. Running agents on a remote box, over a link you don’t trust:

Your connection drops mid-task, you run the same command again, and you’re back in the same session with the agent still going. Pair it with mosh if your link is bad enough that SSH itself keeps dying.

The nested-tmux problem: if you run tmux locally and also on the remote box, both grab the same prefix. The two fixes are a different prefix on the remote ( set -g prefix C-a ), or pressing the prefix twice, which bind C-b send-prefix gives you.

For running agents on a machine that isn’t the one in front of you, see remote development .

tmux is good software. It solves multiplexing and persistence about as well as those can be solved, and it has been doing it since 2007. What it doesn’t do is anything specific to agents, because agents didn’t exist when its model was designed.

No visibility into which agent is parked. An agent waiting on an approval prompt looks exactly like an agent thinking, which looks exactly like an agent that finished twenty minutes ago. All three are “a pane with some text in it”. The status-line hack above exists to paper over this, and it papers by scraping.

No notification when one finishes. monitor-silence is the nearest thing, and it fires on any quiet pane for any reason. There is no event for “the agent is done” because tmux has no idea what an agent is.

Screen scraping is brittle by construction. capture-pane gives you the rendered frame: spinners, box drawing, truncated columns, ANSI. Not what the agent said, not which tool it called, not whether that call succeeded. Every parser you write against it breaks when the agent ships a UI change.

No shared state across sessions. Two agents in two tmux sessions have no way to see each other. If you want one to read another’s transcript or hand off work, you build that yourself, out of files and locks and polling.

Scrollback for several streaming agents is expensive. history-limit 100000 across a dozen panes of agent output is real memory, held per pane for as long as the server lives, and gone the moment it does. See terminal emulators for AI agents for why the rendering side of this gets costly too.

items.title: L’economia cinese è cresciuta più del previsto nel terzo trimestre del 2026, soprattutto grazie alle esportazioni
items.content:
Nel terzo trimestre del 2026 il prodotto interno lordo (PIL) della Cina è cresciuto del 4,5 per cento rispetto allo stesso periodo dell’anno precedente, secondo i dati diffusi lunedì dall’Ufficio nazionale di statistica cinese. È un leggero miglioramento rispetto al 4,3 per cento del secondo trimestre dell’anno, quando la crescita dell’economia cinese era stata la più bassa da oltre tre anni , ed è superiore alle previsioni degli analisti, che si aspettavano il 4,4 per cento. Nel primo trimestre l’economia era cresciuta del 5 per cento.

La crescita è stata sostenuta soprattutto dalle esportazioni: in particolare sono aumentate le vendite all’estero di semiconduttori e altri prodotti tecnologici, per la forte domanda mondiale legata allo sviluppo dell’intelligenza artificiale, ma anche quelle di automobili elettriche e ibride. Continuano però le difficoltà dell’economia interna: i consumi rimangono deboli e tra gennaio e settembre gli investimenti immobiliari sono diminuiti del 20,6 per cento rispetto allo stesso periodo del 2025. Complessivamente, nei primi nove mesi del 2026 l’economia cinese è cresciuta del 4,6 per cento. Il governo ha fissato per quest’anno un obiettivo tra il 4,5 e il 5 per cento. I dati economici diffusi dal governo cinese vanno però presi con cautela: la loro attendibilità è da tempo messa in discussione dagli economisti, anche per la scarsa trasparenza delle statistiche ufficiali e le difficoltà nel verificarle in modo indipendente.

items.title: Flatpak – An Insecurity Nightmare
items.summary: Article URL: https://oro.gay/posts/flatpak-an-insecurity-nightmare/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50148601 Points: 52 # Comments: 42
items.content:
For over 20 years, Linux has been used everywhere, from servers to embedded devices. One area it has been lacking in, however, is the desktop space. Windows and macOS have constantly been keeping Linux out of the market, with gaming primarily being a Windows thing and content creators utilizing macOS.

Over the last decade, the Linux desktop has been improving dramatically: Flatpak, Wayland, Portals, PipeWire, and FreeDesktop have all been working to make Linux an operating system better suited to modern (desktop) systems. I'm not going to go over all of those though; as you could probably tell by the title, this is going to be about Flatpak!

Let's take a quick look at the server space. It's not uncommon to see them running decade-old (sometimes even decades -old!) kernels and libraries. This makes sense, as their boot times are long and on every single system update, there's a risk of breakage, and needing to debug that; valuable uptime lost, especially for a service as large as Google. Naturally, they evolved a way to quickly patch the most relevant parts of the system, so security isn't too much of an issue.

However, the software they run may only be able to utilize newer features from newer libraries, not the old and crusty software the servers run. So how did they solve that?

Containers. Normally used to ship software to several customers in a consistent and safer way, they allow you to isolate software into a little box with all of the needed dependencies, at their specified versions, with limited access to the host system.

We have Android, macOS, and iOS, all with limited access to the system, requiring end-user intervention to access certain resources. But what about the Linux desktop?

In 2015, Flatpak was released, taking all of the technology used from containerization on servers, and applying it to desktop systems. With it came Portals , and the Freedesktop SDK . This gave a consistent and generic platform and API to developers, a drastic change from what was previously a battleground of varying dependency versions, core system libraries, and packaging formats.

Of course, after having the distribution and development situation stay the same for a few decades, this was too large of a change to make at once. Many of the needed APIs exist, but developers need to take time out of their day to migrate to them, and some users (specifically, Flatpak-hating ones) vehemently refuse to help improve the situation, insisting we stick with the old way of doing things, and repackage software hundreds of times for thousands of varying systems.

To put it simply, naturally, nobody in their right mind gave a shit. Many new application developers are creating their apps with a confined environment in mind, and shipping their software to Flathub, allowing the software to get to end users in a fast and secure way.

What about the old applications, though? You can find 10-year-old apps shipped on Flathub, after all. From these applications spawned articles such as Flatpak - a security nightmare hey, you might recognize that name! , and various responses from well-known individuals within the FOSS space intended to counteract misinformation and aggression from those articles.

For these apps, the FUD (fear, uncertainty, and doubt) articles like to cherry-pick the worst offenders and use this to say that Flatpak isn't worth pushing for at all. So I'd like to address that.

These applications were designed with an unconfined environment, and the APIs necessary for them either didn't exist at the time or they weren't updated to use the new API. Cherry-picking them to show that the Flatpak sandbox is "not a sandbox" is not a valid argument, and only shows that the applications themselves are insecure.

Of course, older apps aren't the only offenders. As the new APIs might not be mature enough, both newer and older apps may have to resort to static permissions in order to work properly. For most newer applications, this is fine, as they can restrict their permissions a lot more than older applications would be able to.

Flatpak is a sandbox. And Flatpak is secure. The applications are not . It doesn't help anyone to change the meaning of the word "sandbox". Just because the sandbox that some apps use isn't on par with iOS or Android, it doesn't disqualify it as a sandbox. If you'd like to blame Flatpak for that, don't be my guest. The fact that the apps rely on static permissions shows that the applications are insecure and rely on inconsistent interfaces, and in some cases, that the current APIs have yet to improve enough for their use cases . We should be focusing on improving that situation, not trying to tear it down.

If you want a real-world example of how a partial sandbox is still effective: the "fractureiser" malware . Even if the malware was nonfunctional on Linux in the first place, it's still an example of how traditional packaging fails to address the fact that modern desktop systems have plenty of ways for a system to be compromised. Running software "that you trust" isn't enough to protect yourself. To quote the relevant notes from the linked post:

If you use Linux, use the PrismLauncher Flatpak and be very careful of what you give it access to through utilities such as Flatseal. By default, it has no access to the needed directories to compromise the system.

Taking a quick look over the decompiled source code, it will indeed fail to function inside of the default PrismLauncher Flatpak sandbox; the current malware hardcodes the user's ~/.config/ directory. The creation of files inside of the Flatpak sandbox, if the app does not have access to that real path, will result in it being written to a tmpfs that gets wiped on a sandbox restart. systemd is also not available inside of the Flatpak sandbox, so executing that command will fail. The malware seems to not attempt to work around these limitations, and assumes it is running unsandboxed.

For a more in-depth view of static permissions and Portals, see Overview of Flatpak’s Permission Models by TheEvilSkeleton .

Some also like to bring up outdated dependencies to the argument. No, this doesn't matter. The runtime itself is updated whenever a needed security update is available (sometimes even breaking the ABI if it's a big enough deal) and application developers don't have to think about manually updating bundled dependencies with automatic update checking . And many major libraries, such as your GPU drivers, can be updated separately from your runtime if you so choose. Outdated dependencies isn't even an argument in the first place.

In the event an application does use outdated libraries, be it because an update broke the build process or the developer forgot to set up the data checker, there is the sandbox placed around all Flatpak applications that can help mitigate these issues while the developer addresses them.

The hope is for the Linux desktop to migrate to developer- and more sandbox-friendly methods of software distribution and programming. We've already made great strides with PipeWire, which paves the way for many nice features with audio and video (including several apps using your camera at the same time!), and FreeDesktop, but we undoubtedly have a ways to go before Linux is a viable platform for developers to target and ship software to.

We can't move forward without modern software like Wayland and Flatpak, no matter how much one might want to repair the situation with Xorg and traditional packaging. If we keep trying to revert to the old way of doing things, all that's shown to developers is that Linux isn't a platform worth considering, and it ends up being a worse situation for end users; turning back into a "which came first: the chicken or the egg?" situation, and resulting in a very bad UX.

If you want more information on Flatpak and in general more information on how it works and the current situation, the following articles are worth a read:

Traditional Packaging is not Suitable for Modern Applications - TheEvilSkeleton

Response to “Developers are lazy, thus Flatpak” - TheEvilSkeleton

Distribution packaging for Linux desktop applications is unsustainable - memoryfile

items.title: L’Ucraina ha ricominciato a ricevere informazioni d’intelligence statunitensi
items.summary: Trump è però tornato ad accusare Zelensky di non volere la pace, e restano limitazioni sulla versione militare di Starlink
items.content:
Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha detto in un’intervista alla rete americana NBC che gli Stati Uniti hanno ricominciato a condividere informazioni d’intelligence con l’Ucraina. Queste informazioni sono essenziali per rilevare gli attacchi missilistici russi con preavviso sufficiente ad allertare la popolazione e limitare i danni: Zelensky si era lamentato per l’interruzione della condivisione la settimana scorsa.

Zelensky ha detto che però rimangono limitazioni su Starshield : è la versione militare del servizio di connessione internet satellitare Starlink, fornito da SpaceX di Elon Musk e gestito dal dipartimento della Difesa statunitense. Zelensky ha riferito che tuttora i terminali smettono di funzionare oltre i 160 chilometri orari, con ripercussioni soprattutto sulle operazioni coi droni. Non si sa ancora chi abbia ordinato le limitazioni: Zelensky ha detto che pensa siano coinvolti sia Musk che l’amministrazione Trump, che in questi giorni ha negato.

Nel frattempo Donald Trump ha scritto un post sul suo social Truth in cui sostiene – come ha fatto altre volte in passato – ci siano progressi nelle trattative con la Russia e accusa nuovamente Zelensky, prendendo le parti del presidente russo Vladimir Putin: «Con tutti i soldi che l’Europa gli sta notoriamente dando, e che l’amministrazione Biden gli ha dato in passato, non vuole finisca questa guerra, e probabilmente non l’ha mai voluto», ha scritto riferendosi al presidente ucraino.

Trump ha sostenuto che le sue iniziative, come l’accordo per aumentare le esportazioni di gasolio russo, servano a non allontanare Putin dalle trattative, che in realtà sono ferme proprio per il massimalismo di Putin. Peraltro, secondo ricostruzioni del Wall Street Journal , Putin ha proposto a Trump un incontro negoziale sull’Ucraina insieme al presidente cinese Xi Jinping, ma senza includere Zelensky.

Le relazioni tra Trump e Zelensky sono in un momentaccio : Trump era arrivato a chiedere esplicitamente la sua sostituzione, e Zelensky aveva detto di sentirsi tradito da lui . Domenica, in un’intervista a Bloomberg , Zelensky ha accusato Trump di volerlo costringere ad arrendersi alla Russia. Ha sostenuto anche di avergli proposto di interrompere gli attacchi alle raffinerie russe in cambio di forniture di intercettori Patriot, di cui l’Ucraina è a corto .

Nella notte ci sono stati nuovi attacchi aerei russi contro la capitale Kyiv, che hanno ucciso almeno una persona. Zelensky ha detto che, nel complesso, sono stati rilevati 16 missili balistici e più di 200 droni, e che gli attacchi russi hanno colpito una decina di infrastrutture energetiche, lasciando senza corrente elettrica almeno 550mila case.

items.title: Australian Greens senator denies claims of misconduct towards women
items.summary: Jordon Steele-John says the timing of the claims is motivated by "nasty political games" within the Greens.
items.content:
An Australian Greens senator has denied allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women and accused his party of "nasty political games", days after the claims emerged.

Last Thursday, Greens leader David Shoebridge said Senator Jordon Steele-John, 32, had taken leave from the party room after a letter from seven current and former members said he had been accused of "multiple allegations" of misconduct between 2017 and 2025.

In an online post on Sunday, the senator denied the claims and said he was not on leave. On a sexual assault claim, he said police investigating the matter had closed the case and no charges were laid.

An internal party probe has been launched into the allegations.

Steele-John, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair, was first elected to the senate in Western Australia in November 2017.

In his letter responding to the claims, Steele-John said his nickname - "Feels on wheels" - initially referred to him being emotional when advocating for disability rights but had since taken on a "more sinister meaning" about his alleged mistreatment of women.

He accused Shoebridge of mishandling the matter and questioned the timing of the letter, saying "it is no coincidence" that the allegations were sent to the leader "the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection" ahead of the next federal election.

Days after the letter with the claims was sent to Shoebridge, local media reported that the party had created a 47-page dossier years earlier that listed a number of allegations against Steele-John and how to manage media coverage if they emerged.

Steele-John said the dossier was made so that the media would not "bombard" the two women at the centre of those claims and that neither woman had made a complaint.

He acknowledged the allegations against him would have "damaged" the public's trust in him and said he was "committed to rebuilding that by acting with as much transparency and accountability as I can".

Shoebridge's office confirmed that the allegations had been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.

A spokesperson for Shoebridge said the leader still believed "leave is appropriate under the circumstances" and taking leave would not influence the internal party investigation.

items.title: In Francia sono state fermate quasi 2.400 persone durante le proteste di sabato, e circa mille poliziotti sono rimasti feriti
items.content:
Il ministero dell’Interno francese ha diffuso un nuovo bilancio delle violenze avvenute sabato durante le grandi manifestazioni contro il carovita nel paese: 2.397 persone sono state fermate, e 997 tra poliziotti e gendarmi sono rimasti feriti, sette dei quali in modo grave. Il bilancio è molto più alto di quello provvisorio comunicato sabato sera, quando il governo aveva parlato di 1.200 fermi e 150 agenti feriti. Non tutte le persone fermate dalla polizia per accertamenti sono state poi arrestate o trattenute in custodia

Le manifestazioni, a cui secondo il governo hanno partecipato circa 550mila persone, erano degenerate in scontri con la polizia, saccheggi e incendi in diverse città, tra cui Parigi, Lione e Marsiglia. Partecipavano non solo gli studenti, che protestano già da giorni , ma anche sindacati, partiti politici ed esponenti del movimento dei “gilet gialli” , che otto anni fa organizzò in tutta la Francia proteste molto estese.

Nuovi scontri si sono verificati anche domenica a Parigi, soprattutto nella zona di Place de la République, dove centinaia di persone si erano radunate nonostante il grande dispiegamento di polizia. Gli agenti hanno usato gas lacrimogeni e granate assordanti per disperdere la folla, mentre gruppi di persone hanno lanciato oggetti contro le forze dell’ordine e saccheggiato alcuni negozi nelle strade vicine. Le violenze sono proseguite anche in serata.

In un discorso alla nazione tenuto domenica sera, il presidente francese Emmanuel Macron ha detto che, in risposta alle violenze, nei prossimi giorni i prefetti potrebbero vietare «alcune manifestazioni» per proteggere le città.

items.title: The EU energy battle rages on — and Italy is losing
items.summary: Brussels agrees to temporary energy bill relief measures, but Meloni fails to secure changes to the EU’s emissions trading system. Now she is pushing for greater flexibility on Italy’s deficit
items.content:
BRUSSELS — No middle ground has been found on European energy policy, leaving Italy with little more than a token concession. Overnight between Thursday and Friday, the European Council reached an agreement on its final summit conclusions, though in reality, the text serves as little more than a formal acknowledgment of unresolved deadlock.

Italy, alongside six other member states — Greece, Cyprus, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia, and the Czech Republic — had pressed for immediate, short-term interventions to lower petrol and gas prices. For Rome, long-term visions are secondary; the crisis is unfolding right now.Italy continues to face some of the highest energy prices in Europe — particularly for natural gas, which costs nearly twice as much as in Spain and a third more than in Germany. Consequently, Rome bears a disproportionate burden in the current energy crunch, compounded by long-standing structural delays in rolling out renewable energy.The compromise wording in the final text fails to defuse the conflict, offering Italy and its allies virtually no tangible gains.

At the core of the dispute remains the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), under which companies purchase carbon allowances for the right to pollute. The system has also been used by the EU to finance the green transition.Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni pressed for a revision of the mechanism, particularly the trading of allowances on the secondary market, which drives up prices and increases costs for businesses. Rome also sought to postpone the implementation of ETS2 — set to take effect in 2028 and extend carbon pricing to building heating and road transport — a request that was firmly rejected.

The diplomatic impasse was formally bypassed with a vague clause in the final declaration, which "invites the Commission to update the assessment of all impacts of the system, paying particular attention to its design and relevant safeguards."

Crucially, however, the text omits any reference to the specific "economic and social" repercussions that the blocking minority had repeatedly highlighted. The document concludes with a generic nod toward the "crucial importance of addressing high energy prices."

There was, however, some good news for Meloni: the European Commission approved temporary measures to ease Italy’s soaring energy bills, allowing the government to offset higher gas costs. Meloni hailed the decision as "another important achievement for Italy", although the relief does not cover the costs associated with the EU’s emissions trading system.

The Meloni-led coalition had held out hope for temporary regulatory exemptions, none of which materialized. The Italian Prime Minister advocated for direct interventions to curb pump prices for fuel and natural gas. These proposals met fierce resistance from Northern Europe's fiscal hawks, who suspect Italy of attempting to dismantle the broader EU decarbonization agenda.Instead, the Council confirmed that only state aid measures would be permitted. The practical upshot is stark: nations with deep pockets, such as Germany, can afford to slash fuel excise duties to shield their citizens, whereas heavily indebted nations like Italy lack the fiscal headroom to utilize such measures.

Lastly, Prime Minister Meloni tabled a request before the European Council for "additional deficit flexibility" to cushion the blow of inflationary shocks. However, the 27 leaders have not considered the proposal for now, leaving it to the European Commission to examine in the coming months.

The widening rift between the fiscal hawks and the "cohesion" bloc is equally evident in discussions surrounding the EU’s upcoming Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). While Northern nations are demanding budget cuts amounting to hundreds of billions of euros, Southern and Eastern states are pushing for an expansion — a path that currently appears all but blocked.With the European political calendar shifting into election season, the battle over energy is set to escalate in the coming weeks. For Italy, where voters head to the polls next year, the political stakes could not be higher.

items.title: The battle for green gold: “Foreign olive oil sold as Italian while ours sits in tanks”
items.summary: Extra virgin olive oil is hitting shelves at very low prices, putting domestic producers under pressure
items.content:
The language farmers use when protesting can sound melodramatic. “Harvest season is about to begin, and we can no longer afford to harvest tears,” one farmer proclaimed from the stage in Piazza Prefettura in Bari, where the first demonstration took place last Monday.

But this time, there is no exaggeration. According to figures certified by the Ministry of Agriculture, 195,044 tons of extra virgin olive oil remain in storage tanks—a 46.7% increase compared to a year ago.

More than half of these stockpiles are concentrated in the South, particularly in Puglia and Calabria, as well as in Tuscany. According to producers, the fault lies in the weaknesses of the "Made in Italy" system, so proudly championed by the Minister of Agriculture, Food Sovereignty and Forestry, Francesco Lollobrigida. The undeniable reality is that storage tanks are full, and last year’s production simply cannot be cleared.

While extra virgin prices were soaring as high as 10 euros per kilogram until January (the wholesale market measures oil by weight, not volume), prices have now plunged to 4 euros on the market in Foggia, according to figures from ISMEA, the institute for agricultural and food market services.

As a result, mill owners—who typically buy olives well in advance—have become heavily overextended with their banks. Having purchased olives at prices far higher than what the oil can fetch today, they are now refusing to buy from growers as the new harvest gets underway, leaving farmers equally stranded.

Rallied under the evocative name Orgoglio Olivicolo ("Olive-Growing Pride"), the farmers are demanding an "extraordinary banking moratorium"—a measure that can only be granted if the government declares a state of agricultural crisis. “We’ve been asking for this since March,” says Gennaro Sicolo, regional director of CIA - Italian Farmers in Puglia.

The most pressing demand is voiced by the elderly Count Onofrio Spagnoletti Zeuli, heir to a historic landowning family from Andria: “We need strict inspections. Too many crooks are importing substandard oil, mixing it with our oil, and passing it off as extra virgin.” It is a form of agricultural xenophobia directed against non-EU oils that, entering the market at bargain prices, have dragged down the value of domestic oil as well.

Francesco Paolicelli, the regional commissioner for agriculture, is pushing for electronic documentation to improve the traceability of the product’s origin.

Meanwhile, Vito Leccese, the Mayor of Bari—directly challenged by protesting farmers to “go check what’s actually being sold in supermarkets”—has written to the head of the local health authority (ASL), calling for an "extraordinary campaign of sampling and analysis of extra virgin olive oil sold in Bari, with inspections at both major retailers and neighborhood shops, starting with 100% Italian oils sold at unusually low prices."

He is also asking for checks on pesticide residues—another suspicion raised by olive growers, who fear chemical levels may be higher in oils imported from countries where products banned in Italy are still permitted.

Yet to find the main culprit behind Italy’s olive oil crisis, one might need to look to Spain rather than Tunisia. Two years ago, a severe drought crippled Spanish production, giving Italian competitors a temporary boost. Today, Spain’s highly mechanized olive sector has rebounded in a major way.

“In the upcoming season,” explains Dora De Santis, representative of the Italian Olive Oil Industry Association, “production is projected to reach 1.6 million tons. This has brought trading of our product to a complete standstill.”

The result is an enormous price gap on supermarket shelves between Italian oils and those from other EU countries. Italian oils, which have significantly higher production costs, sell for twice as the price of their European counterparts. “We have asked major retailers to communicate more effectively to consumers the added value behind that price difference,” says De Santis.

Meanwhile, Maria Lisa Clodoveo, a professor of food technology, defends Tunisian oil: “Ninety-five percent of their olive cultivation is traditional, using minimal chemical fertilizers.”

items.title: Hopper’s America in Pisa: thesis, antithesis and synthesis
items.summary: An exhibition in the Tuscan city brings together works by the American artist who captured urban nights, dawn over the ocean and the loneliness of the forgotten — and made his wife both his muse and his victim
items.content:
Anyone lucky enough to visit the Edward Hopper exhibition in Pisa should keep a few things in mind — and enjoy the experience. Essentially: three theses, their antitheses and the inevitable synthesis.

The first is that Hopper is the poet, even before he is the painter, of American loneliness: of the emptiness that emerges not in the boundless expanses of the prairies or among the mountains of the country’s interior, but in the far vaster and deeper void that opens up in the cities of the East Coast, whether the metropolis of New York or some little-known New England town caught in the drowsy light of an ordinary dawn.

It is there that he places his men and women, their eyes cast down, fixed on some inanimate object or simply staring nowhere. And it is there that he abandons them: lost figures.

The second is that in a great many of these paintings, the female figure portrayed or transformed is his wife, Jo — Josephine Nivison — his companion for 60 years of his life, who outlived him by just ten months and who, by their silver wedding anniversary, was already writing to him: “We deserve the Croix de Guerre for distinguished service in battle.”

We see her slender as she was not, sitting on an unmade bed; or voluptuous as she was, in an office beside the desk of a colleague or boss, looking at a sheet of paper on the floor and preparing to pick it up with a gesture whose barely nascent sensuality taps at the viewer’s mind. His muse, his agent, his beloved and irreplaceable enemy.

The third is that these characters — the late-night customers in a nameless bar, the people using vending machines in the middle of nowhere — are the “forgotten men (and women)” upon whom, as Ezio Mauro argued in his 2018 essay L’uomo bianco , the electoral success of the man furthest removed from that category, Donald Trump, was built through the most cynical of deceptions.

So much for the three theses. Now prepare for the antitheses.

First antithesis: in reality, Hopper spares his figures the sentence of loneliness, carrying them beyond its threshold.

That is the argument Antonio Spadaro makes in his book Oltrecolore . What isolates them, in fact, is the widespread assumption that meaning lies in the single moment, rather than the course of events in which that moment unfolds.

As if switching on a light and revealing the solution to a mystery, Spadaro writes instead that “in Hopper’s paintings, figures are caught waiting for something to happen, as though a revelation were within reach. The answer lies beyond the surface of the painting. The resolution of that waiting is not given, but suggested as something inevitable. There is a certainty that something must happen or someone must arrive, even though we do not know what or who. Hopper is therefore the master who knows how to capture the unstable instant in which life reveals itself as a desire for some form of salvation.”

According to this antithesis, the woman on the bed in Morning Sun is not alone. She is simply waiting: for a distant lover, for forgiveness, for the telephone to ring, for us — who, year after year after year, will come to keep her company, caressing her with our gaze.

Second antithesis: that woman is none other than Jo, hidden behind the greatness of her husband.

She, too, was a painter — and he took the brush from her hand. Invited to exhibit at the Brooklyn Museum alongside the emerging artists of the day, she persuaded the museum to find room for him as well, helping to launch his career.

She settled for posing, promoting him and suggesting titles — Nighthawks was her title too. She accepted living in the shadows of those paintings filled with light. She saw him send her cat away and forbid her from driving. And yet, mysteriously, she never stopped loving and hating him — but above all, loving him.

Third antithesis: Hopper was not thinking about the forgotten, the dispossessed, those left behind on the road to prosperity. He was no revolutionary, reformer or progressive.

He accepted the world as it was, America as it was. He put himself in his subjects’ shoes — he is one of the nighthawks, just as he appears in other paintings — but without empathy. Whether he was registering an absence or heralding a presence, for him it was an artistic question, never an ideological one.

So, whether you love cats or women’s emancipation, whether you believe in revelations or are a pessimist, whether you are for or against Trump, make your synthesis — and then forget it.

items.title: Smoking guns at the opera
items.summary: “Writing for the cinema is a habit I can’t kick,” says composer Nicola Piovani. For now, though, he is turning Romanzo criminale into an opera, with a libretto by Giancarlo De Cataldo. “Opera plots are often confusing. Not this time.”
items.content:
Nicola Piovani is a musician who is both serious and light-hearted, profound and irreverent in the way the most authentic Romans often are, with a formidable cultural background but never a hint of pedantry or pretension. As a composer, he has a strong ironic streak, though that does not make him any less attuned to the great questions of human existence. He moves skilfully between different styles while retaining a distinctive and original voice.

The composer of celebrated film scores — he won an Oscar for Roberto Benigni’s Life Is Beautiful , among many other accolades — Piovani has a particular love of musical theatre.

“The combination of poetry, singing and dramatic action, together with the colours of the orchestra, exerts a feverish, celestial fascination over me,” he says ahead of his third premiere in the genre, following the operas Amorosa presenza (2022) and Il labirinto di Creta (2024).

Now he is venturing, dangerously enough — La musica è pericolosa , Music Is Dangerous, is the title of both one of his books and a successful stage show — into the aggressive strategies and complex characters of Romanzo criminale . The opera is based on Giancarlo De Cataldo’s bestselling novel, with De Cataldo himself writing the libretto.

The themes and fate of this popular saga are well known. It began as a novel about the bloody history of the Banda della Magliana, the criminal gang that dominated Rome’s underworld for more than a decade from the 1970s onwards, and became a landmark of Italian noir, spawning a film directed by Michele Placido and two Sky television series.

Piovani accepted an invitation from Carlo Fuortes, superintendent of Florence’s Teatro del Maggio Musicale Fiorentino, where the opera opens on October 23 and runs until October 31. Co-produced by Fondazione Musica per Roma, it will be staged again next year in the capital at the Auditorium Parco della Musica.

Piovani himself will conduct, with Massimo Popolizio directing and sets by Margherita Palli.

“Usually, when I compose music that isn’t for the cinema, I choose the subject myself,” Piovani says. “This time, however, the idea came from Fuortes, who persuaded me to set an already defined project to music. I agreed after a very good meeting with De Cataldo, who is an opera aficionado and understands how different a libretto is from either a novel or a screenplay.”

“First of all, by creating a structure divided into 21 theatrical scenes. De Cataldo gave me a draft from which I took verses, lines and situations and began setting them to music. Each time, he would go back over the material in his elegant style, while also accommodating the constraints imposed by the music. He immersed himself skilfully in writing in verse, metre and rhyme, as singing requires.”

“Yes, it’s ideal material. There’s a love triangle involving the criminal Dandi, a tenor; the prostitute Patrizia, a soprano; and the police officer Scialoia, another tenor, who wants to redeem her. There’s Dandi’s betrayal of Bufalo, a baritone, and Bufalo’s revenge on Dandi. There’s a duet between Libanese, a tenor, and his mother, a mezzo-soprano. Libanese even rises from the grave to take revenge, like the Commendatore in Don Giovanni .”

“It’s symphonic and classical, with some additional instruments: drums, electronic drums, saxophone and a keyboard that reproduces sampled sounds. In our case, those are gunshots and sirens, all written into the score.”

“What seemed most suited to music was the fable behind the story, almost a parable: four young men want to become rich to escape a frustrating social condition. They take a violent shortcut, they win and seize power: ‘They ascend the throne,’ as the libretto puts it. From there begins a downward spiral in which everyone loses and everyone dies except one, Freddo, who no longer wants to live surrounded by blood. He is the most introspective character. He decides to put an end to his adventurous life before the adventure puts an end to him. He leaves, but we don’t know where he goes. He simply disappears.”

“I fell in love with the prostitute Patrizia. She isn’t a heroine, but a gentle soul cloaked in the cynicism instilled in her by a childhood scarred by humiliation. She is the one who tells us the story and draws together the threads of the parable about four friends who wanted to conquer the world and came to a bad end. My music leans on her to convey the emotional meaning of the whole story. Her singing has a mocking quality that at times soars into flashes of passionate lyricism.”

Did you have any historical reference points when composing the score?

“I stayed away from verismo, naturalism, dialect and Brechtianism. Inside and behind this novel, as I said, there is a cruel and compelling fable. We tried to translate that into verse and music, and as I wrote I remained faithful to the stylistic path that feels most naturally mine. Today, the theoretical and ideological choices of the late 20th-century classical repertoire strike me as a senseless relic. I have always been wary of the high priests of experimentation at Darmstadt, and all the more so today: 80 years later, those stylistic conventions hold no interest for me.

"That said, everyone should compose whatever music they want. I try to write music that reflects who I am, intimately and honestly. If I write ugly music, then I suppose I must be ugly too. I consider the paths taken by Britten, Shostakovich, Rota, Bernstein and Weill indispensable, but also those of Lennon and McCartney and Dave Brubeck. At the moment, I particularly enjoy listening to Valentin Silvestrov. Until just a few years ago, tonal music was blacklisted by the dominant culture. Now some people would like to blacklist post-serialism. The only thing I would blacklist is the blacklist itself, an unbearable affectation of so much 20th-century intelligentsia.”

In the novel, the gang’s criminal activities are intertwined with the country’s political life. Have you retained that aspect?

“Rome — eternal Rome, De Cataldo’s Rome — is the backdrop to this operatic fable. But we never delve into the specific events of the period. Rome is sung as a metaphor, and Patrizia, who opens and closes the narrative, echoes the image of the she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus.”

Can you give us any idea of what to expect from Popolizio’s production?

“The setting isn’t naturalistic, but it clearly shows the progression of the plot, which is what I always want from directors, including those tackling works from the classical repertoire. Opera plots can be complicated or confusing. Someone seeing Verdi’s Il Trovatore for the first time should be helped by the direction to understand the different turns and episodes in the story. Instead, directors sometimes seem to enjoy obscuring the development of the action with distracting effects that have little or nothing to do with the narrative.”

“I’ve written scores for more than 200 films, neglecting my vocation for symphonic and chamber music, as well as opera. In recent years, I’ve tried to redress the balance. But writing music for the cinema is a habit you never quite kick. From November, I’ll be working on Oliva Denaro , directed by Cristina Comencini, and Chiles rellenos , by Guatemalan director Robert Flanagan.”

items.title: L’impennata dell’inflazione è una pessima notizia per Trump
items.summary: L’aumento dei prezzi dell’energia e di altri beni di uso quotidiano sta mettendo in grande difficoltà il presidente degli Stati Uniti e il Partito repubblicano in vista delle elezioni di metà mandato Leggi
items.content:
“Il presidente Donald Trump e i repubblicani hanno appena ricevuto la peggiore notizia possibile sull’inflazione a pochi giorni dalle elezioni di metà mandato: a settembre i prezzi sono aumentati più del previsto”, afferma la Cnn . “Gli elettori statunitensi non sono rimasti certo sorpresi. Come mostrano i sondaggi, sono furiosi per l’alto costo della vita, che persiste dai tempi della pandemia ma che nell’ultimo anno è stato aggravato dalle politiche di Trump, tra cui i dazi doganali e, soprattutto, la guerra in Iran”.

Secondo un sondaggio condotto dal canale televisivo Fox News , l’85 per cento degli elettori è preoccupato per l’inflazione e l’83 per cento per i prezzi della benzina. L’unica preoccupazione più grande è la corruzione politica (88 per cento).

In base ai dati ufficiali pubblicati il 14 ottobre, negli Stati Uniti l’inflazione ha subìto una forte accelerazione a settembre, trainata dai prezzi dell’energia. L’aumento su base annua è stato del 3,7 per cento, contro il 3,4 per cento di agosto.

Più nel dettaglio, i prezzi della benzina sono aumentati del 9 per cento rispetto ad agosto e del 34 per cento su base annua, mentre quelli dell’olio combustibile, usato per riscaldare le case, sono saliti del 15 per cento rispetto ad agosto e del 74 per cento su base annua.

Oltre a erodere gli stipendi, l’impennata dell’inflazione potrebbe spingere la Fed, la banca centrale degli Stati Uniti, a procedere a un secondo aumento consecutivo dei tassi d’interesse in occasione di una riunione di politica monetaria prevista alla fine di ottobre. Un eventuale aumento renderebbe il credito più costoso, aggravando le difficoltà delle famiglie.

Il New York Times sottolinea che “la maggior parte dell’aumento dei prezzi deriva direttamente da quelli dell’energia, che quest’anno sono saliti alle stelle a causa della guerra in Iran. L’offensiva militare degli Stati Uniti si è tradotta in un aumento dei costi per i cittadini, che pagano di più per fare il pieno, riscaldare le case e viaggiare in aereo”.

“Ma il conflitto in Iran, e lo shock energetico che ne è seguito, non è l’unico responsabile delle pressioni sui prezzi”, prosegue il giornale. “I dazi imposti da Trump hanno reso più costosi molti prodotti di uso quotidiano, tra cui gli elettrodomestici. Anche il boom degli investimenti nel settore dell’intelligenza artificiale ha contribuito al rialzo dell’inflazione, facendo aumentare i prezzi dei computer e delle apparecchiature digitali quasi del 10 per cento nell’ultimo anno, e quelli dei software addirittura del 28 per cento”.

Secondo il Washington Post , le difficoltà economiche delle famiglie statunitensi dipendono anche da un fattore poco considerato: i debiti: “Nuovi dati dimostrano che le rate mensili per comprare un auto e per i prestiti studenteschi hanno raggiunto livelli record, e stanno gravando pesantemente sui bilanci delle famiglie”. Si stima che più di un terzo degli adulti statunitensi stia pagando le rate di un prestito per l’auto o di un debito studentesco.

“Per alleviare gli effetti dell’inflazione, nelle ultime settimane l’amministrazione Trump ha attinto a piene mani dalla sua borsa dei trucchi”, afferma la Cnn . “In una mossa disperata, all’inizio di ottobre Trump ha perfino annunciato un accordo controverso con la Russia che prevede la revoca di alcune sanzioni per poter importare una quantità relativamente modesta di gasolio russo”.

Ma secondo il New York Times difficilmente l’accordo farà scendere il prezzi del gasolio, che si è impennato a causa della guerra in Iran e degli attacchi ucraini alle raffinerie russe.

“Secondo alcuni esperti del settore dell’energia, la quantità di gasolio che la Russia fornirebbe è nettamente inferiore rispetto a quella che Mosca esportava nello stesso periodo del 2025, e rappresenta solo una piccola parte dell’approvvigionamento perso nel mondo a causa della decisione di Trump di attaccare l’Iran. Inoltre, non è chiaro se la Russia sia effettivamente in grado di fornire il carburante promesso”, spiega il quotidiano statunitense, riferendosi ai danni inflitti alle raffinerie russe dagli attacchi ucraini. Per ripararli potrebbero infatti volerci mesi o anni.

Il canale televisivo canadese Cbc sottolinea che i dati sull’inflazione complicheranno sicuramente le cose per Trump e per il Partito repubblicano, che potrebbero perdere il controllo del congresso nelle elezioni di metà mandato del 3 novembre.

“Sono proprio le conseguenze politiche dell’inflazione ad aver spinto Trump ad andare in giro per gli Stati Uniti a sostenere i candidati repubblicani al senato”, prosegue la Cbc. “Nelle ultime due settimane Trump ha visitato una serie di stati tradizionalmente repubblicani, tra cui l’Alaska, il Kansas, l’Ohio e il Texas, in cui nelle presidenziali del 2024 il Partito repubblicano aveva vinto con più di dieci punti di scarto”.

Trump ha liquidato le preoccupazioni per il costo della vita definendole una “montatura dei democratici”, sostenendo inoltre che l’inflazione sia migliorata durante il suo mandato, un’affermazione falsa.

Ma come indicano i sondaggi, le argomentazioni di Trump non sembrano aver convinto gli elettori. Secondo il Silver Bulletin , un aggregatore di sondaggi, più del 70 per cento degli intervistati disapprova il modo in cui il governo ha gestito l’inflazione.

Il Partito democratico ha avuto buon gioco a denunciare “il fallimento totale” di Trump sull’inflazione, afferma Fox Business , che riporta le dichiarazioni dell’ex segretario dei trasporti Pete Buttigieg e del leader della minoranza democratica al senato Chuck Schumer.

“L’inflazione sta accelerando, e non a causa di una pandemia o di una catastrofe naturale, ma a causa della guerra di Trump, dei dazi e degli sgravi fiscali per le imprese. È tutto molto chiaro: i repubblicani hanno preso il potere e poi hanno fatto lievitare il costo della vita”, ha dichiarato Buttigieg.

“La cosiddetta ‘età dell’oro’ proclamata da Trump significa prezzi sempre più alti per il popolo statunitense, mentre lui si concede una sala da ballo e i miliardari ottengono sgravi fiscali”, ha scritto invece Schumer su X.

Il quotidiano britannico The Guardian analizza le prospettive elettorali del Partito repubblicano: “A pochi giorni dalle elezioni di metà mandato, Trump e i suoi seguaci sperano che considerazioni ideologiche, in grado di modellare la realtà economica per adattarla alle preferenze politiche, possano impedire una disfatta elettorale. Stanno cercando d’ingannare i sostenitori del movimento Maga facendogli credere che l’economia statunitense sia in ottima salute. Ma stavolta non dovrebbe funzionare, perché i problemi economici sono evidenti anche a molti dei più fervidi seguaci di Trump”.

“Gli abitanti delle zone rurali, per esempio, che votano per i repubblicani da decenni, sono stati messi a dura prova dalle politiche di Trump”, prosegue il giornale. “Sono stati colpiti dalle sue guerre commerciali, che gli hanno impedito l’accesso ai mercati cinesi, ma anche dall’aumento dei prezzi del gasolio e dei fertilizzanti, conseguenza diretta dell’offensiva in Iran. Sono stati messi in difficoltà anche dalle retate dell’amministrazione contro gli immigrati che fanno parte della loro forza lavoro. Infine, si sono sentiti traditi dal tentativo di Trump di frenare l’aumento dei prezzi della carne bovina riducendo i dazi sulle importazioni di carne”.

“Difficilmente”, conclude il Guardian, “Trump riuscirà a convincere gli abitanti delle zone rurali e tutti gli altri elettori che le loro difficoltà sono solo immaginarie”. ◆

items.title: Che aria respiravano i dinosauri?
items.summary: Che aria respiravano i dinosauri?
items.content:
I dinosauri vivevano in un clima molto più ricco di anidride carbonica rispetto a quello odierno. Uno studio delle Università di Göttingen e Mainz (Germania) ha ricostruito la composizione dell'aria del Mesozoico analizzando gli isotopi dell'ossigeno conservati nello smalto di denti fossili.. I risultati indicano che nel Giurassico superiore la concentrazione di CO₂ raggiungeva circa le 1.200 parti per milione, mentre nel tardo Cretaceo questo dato si attestava sulle 750 ppm, contro le circa 430 attuali.. Clima più caldo
Secondo i ricercatori, questi elevati livelli erano alimentati soprattutto dall'intensa attività vulcanica, che immetteva enormi quantità di gas serra nell'atmosfera. Alcuni reperti mostrano bruschi aumenti della CO₂, probabilmente legati a grandi eruzioni.. Una firma chimica nei fossili
Tale tecnica apre una nuova finestra sul passato: i denti dei dinosauri conservano infatti una "firma chimica" dell'aria respirata milioni di anni fa, permettendo di ricostruire il clima e gli ecosistemi in cui vivevano..

items.title: Superlite: A Faster Alternatie to Superpowers
items.summary: Article URL: https://contextfirst.blog/superlite-hand-an-agent-a-spec/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50147492 Points: 99 # Comments: 40
items.content:
I had a dream. I would hand an agent a spec, close the laptop, make a sandwich, and come back to finished, tested, committed work.

Here's what actually happened. I handed over the spec. I made the sandwich. I came back. The agent had written one paragraph and was asking, very politely, whether I approved section 1 of the design.

Section 2. Approve? Yes. Section 3. Approve? Yes. The spec? Yes. The plan? Yes, obviously, it's the plan I just watched you write. And how would I like the plan executed? However is fastest, please, I beg you.

Then it started building. One task. Then a review of that task. Then a fix for the review. Then a re-review of the fix. Then the next task. I watched a progress log scroll past like a train at a level crossing: no stopping it, no getting past it, and no idea how many carriages were left.

I'd refresh the terminal. Still on task 3. I'd answer an email. Still on task 3. I'd start a second sandwich purely to have something to do with my hands. Task 4, under review.

The sandwiches were very good. The software didn't exist yet. And the worst part wasn't the time. It was that I couldn't leave. Every time I walked away, I came back to a question that had been sitting there for twenty minutes, waiting for me to type "yes."

I didn't want a collaborator that needed me every four minutes. I wanted a contractor. Here's the spec, here's the key, call me when it's done.

So I built superlite : a Claude Code plugin that plans a build, splits it into tasks that can run side by side, hands each one to the cheapest agent that can do it well, checks the seams between them, and reviews the result. Then it leaves you a tidy list of every decision it made while you were busy with the sandwich.

This post covers why it exists, how it works, and how to use it. The benchmarks are there to show I'm not just saying it's fast because I wrote it.

First, a disclaimer, because I like this project and don't want angry emails. I use superpowers a lot. It's a careful, collaborative workflow that keeps a human close to every step, and it's genuinely excellent at that. Superlite borrows its bones shamelessly: the plugin layout, the session-start hook, the lifecycle skills. Credit where it's due, and then some.

But when I already knew exactly what I wanted, most of the time went on the workflow waiting for itself. I profiled it, the way you'd check your bank statement after a suspicious weekend. The time went to five places:

None of these are mistakes. Each one is a sensible safety net. Stacked together, they're perfect when you want to steer every step, and slightly maddening when you just want the thing built.

So superlite isn't a rival to superpowers. It's tuned for a different job: autonomous development, at speed. If you want to steer each step, use superpowers. If you want to hand over a spec and come back to working code, use superlite . Just don't enable both in the same session. They share skill names, both inject context at startup, and they argue like siblings in the back seat.

The short version: one approval, a plan written for parallelism, agents matched to the work, and rules enforced by code because, as it turns out, agents read the rules and then do what they like.

One batch of questions, one approval. Superlite sizes the request first. A typo just gets fixed, without a design document about the typo. A change to an existing flow gets a short design in chat. A new project gets one batch of up to four questions, then one design-and-plan document. You approve it once. After that it only stops for things that are destructive, outward-facing or security-sensitive. It won't push to main while you're getting lunch. It will do everything else.

You choose who's in charge. With a human orchestrator, you see the whole plan with its predicted schedule and approve it before anything runs. With an AI orchestrator, you're not needed at all, which is either freeing or mildly insulting depending on your mood. Every choice it would normally ask about gets recorded as a ruling: what it decided, why, and what it costs if it got that wrong. When you come back, you know exactly which decisions to second-guess first.

A plan written for the split. The plan is a task graph. Each task lists the files it owns, the exact interfaces it consumes and produces, and the tests it has to pass. Tasks that don't share files and don't depend on each other run at the same time. The graph decides how wide the build goes. On the current benchmark that peaked at 18 agents working at once, which is roughly the size of a small startup, minus the ping-pong table.

Gated by code, not by prompts. I learned this one the hard way. You can write "the coordinator never edits code" in a prompt in bold, in capitals, with feeling. The coordinator will read it, nod, and edit the code. So now hooks enforce it. One hook blocks the coordinator from editing project code. Another catches any raw pytest or npm test it runs and quietly turns it into a background run, so tests never block it. Another refuses to let anyone kill processes by name (there's a story there, and it's in the deep dive). A plan has to pass lint --stable before work starts, and stable tasks are sent off the moment it passes.

Every run is measured. Hooks record each agent's tokens, cost and time. That feeds the next run's predictions and a soft budget that taps you on the shoulder at 70% of the cap.

You'll need Claude Code, git, Python 3.10 or newer (for superlite's own tools; the project you build can be in any language), and bash (Git Bash on Windows).

The source is iha2/superlite on GitHub. Install it from the marketplace:

Or clone iha2/superlite and load a local checkout for one session:

To check it's working, open a fresh session and send Let's make a react todo list . A working install starts brainstorming before it writes any code. It's the "hello world" of agent workflows, and honestly the world doesn't need another todo list, but it's a good smoke test.

It never pushes or merges without you. Autonomous, not reckless.

Anyone can call their own tool fast. I once called a script I wrote "blazing" and it took eleven minutes to rename some files. So every number below comes from a headless benchmark harness. It builds the same project from the same spec, on Opus, and scores the result with a hidden test suite the agents never get to see. No peeking, no studying for the exam.

The test project is deliberately not a todo list. It's a static site generator plus a spreadsheet engine (formula evaluator, HTTP API and a browser UI) built as one project from one spec, and scored by 177 hidden tests.

Same 177 out of 177 hidden tests, in about half the time. That's one run of the current build against earlier runs on the same machine, so call it a strong hint rather than peer-reviewed science. But it's a very strong hint.

It also beat its own previous build (which averaged 26.9 minutes) by 40%. Yes, I'm competing with my own past self. It's the only rival I can bully freely.

The latest run didn't come out of nowhere. The first build was already quick on a smaller task: sitegen alone, nine modules, 89 hidden tests.

Most of that speed came from getting rid of the queue. Superpowers dispatched 21 agents, one after another. Superlite dispatched 10, up to five at once. Same work, fewer people standing in line.

On the full 177-test project, an earlier superlite build ran three times against superpowers:

Faster on average and much more predictable. A 47-minute worst case is the difference between "done before standup" and "done after standup, during which you had to say it's nearly done."

But the data also showed where superlite was still waiting on itself. The build was finishing at about 13 minutes, and then 10 to 18 more minutes went on reviews, fixes, and the coordinator running tests in the foreground and staring at them. So:

If your agent workflow is slow, it's probably not slow because the model is thinking deep thoughts. It's slow because work is waiting in a line, and something keeps asking permission.

Split the work along interface boundaries. Let independent tasks run at once. Move the mechanical steps into scripts. And enforce the rules that matter with code, because asking nicely only works on people, and only sometimes.

In the follow-up post I go much deeper into the philosophy and the decisions behind superlite: the gates, the agent tiers, and the graveyard of ideas I was very confident about right up until I measured them.

Iheatu Chris Wogu is an engineering manager writing about launch programs, honest metrics, and engineering-led agentic delivery: building delivery systems, then writing down what actually worked.
